Chapter 3
Concerning Mixed Principalities

The real difficulties arise in a new principality. This is especially true if the territory is not entirely new, but rather added to an existing state to form a mixed or composite principality. The instability here stems from a natural problem found in all new conquests. People gladly change their rulers, hoping things will get better. This hope drives them to take up arms against their current leader. But they are fooling themselves. Experience quickly teaches them that things have only gone from bad to worse. This happens because of another inevitable reality: a new prince is always forced to burden his new subjects. He has to quarter his army among them and inflict endless other hardships that come with taking over a new territory.

As a result, you make enemies of everyone you injured while seizing power. At the same time, you cannot keep the friendship of those who helped you get there. You simply cannot satisfy them in the way they expected. Furthermore, you cannot use harsh measures against them because you are indebted to them. No matter how powerful your army is, you always need the goodwill of the locals to successfully enter and hold a province.

This is exactly why King Louis XII of France quickly occupied Milan and just as quickly lost it. The first time, it only took the forces of Duke Lodovico to drive him out. The locals had opened the gates for the French king, but soon realized they were completely deceived in their hopes for future benefits. They simply could not stomach the harsh treatment of their new prince. It is true, however, that when you conquer rebellious provinces a second time, they are much harder to lose. The prince uses the rebellion as an excuse to drop any hesitation. He ruthlessly punishes the guilty, purges anyone he suspects, and fortifies his weakest positions. So, to make France lose Milan the first time, all Duke Lodovico had to do was stir up a few border revolts. But to make France lose it a second time, the whole world had to unite against the king, destroying his armies and driving them entirely out of Italy.
Duke Lodovico was Lodovico Moro, a son of Francesco Sforza, who married Beatrice d’Este. He ruled over Milan from 1494 to 1500, and died in 1510.

Regardless, Milan was stripped from France both the first and the second time. We have already covered the general reasons for the first loss. Now we must look at the reasons for the second. We need to examine what resources the King of France had, and what anyone in his shoes should have done to secure the conquest more effectively than he did.

When a prince conquers new territories and adds them to his original state, these new lands either share the same country and language, or they do not. When they do, they are much easier to hold, especially if the people are not used to governing themselves. To secure them completely, you only need to wipe out the bloodline of the prince who used to rule them. As long as you maintain their old conditions and respect their customs, the two peoples will live quietly together. We have seen this with Brittany, Burgundy, Gascony, and Normandy, which have been tied to France for a very long time. Even if there is a slight difference in language, their customs are similar enough that they can easily get along. If you annex such territories and want to keep them, you only need to remember two rules. First, you must completely extinguish the family of their former lord. Second, you must not change their laws or raise their taxes. If you follow these steps, the new territory will seamlessly merge with your old principality in no time.

But things get messy when you acquire states in a region that has different languages, customs, and laws. To hold them, you need a tremendous amount of luck and relentless energy. One of the best and most effective solutions is for the conquering prince to go and live there in person. This makes the new possession much more secure and durable. It worked for the Turkish Empire in Greece. No matter what other strategies the Turks used to maintain control, they would have lost the territory if the Sultan had not moved there. When you are on the ground, you can spot trouble the moment it starts and crush it instantly. If you are far away, you only hear about the riots when they have grown too large to stop. Furthermore, living there prevents your own officials from looting the country. The locals are happier because they have direct access to you. If they want to be loyal, they have more reason to love you. If they want to rebel, they have more reason to fear you. Any foreign power thinking of attacking that state will have to think twice. As long as you live there, it is almost impossible for anyone to take it from you.

The second and better option is to establish colonies in one or two crucial locations. These colonies act as the keys to the territory. If you do not do this, you will have to station a massive, expensive army of cavalry and infantry there instead. Colonies cost a prince almost nothing. You can send settlers and maintain them with very little expense. The only people you offend are the specific individuals whose lands and houses you confiscate to give to the new settlers. Since these victims are only a small minority, and they are left poor and scattered, they can never organize to threaten you. Everyone else in the territory remains unharmed and is therefore easy to keep quiet. They will also be terrified of stepping out of line, afraid that they will lose their homes just like their neighbors did. In short, these colonies are cheap, highly loyal, and cause minimal disruption. The few people you do injure are left too impoverished and divided to strike back. This brings us to a crucial rule: you must either treat men well or completely crush them. Men can take revenge for minor insults, but if you break them utterly, they cannot fight back. Therefore, if you must injure a man, do it so severely that you never have to fear his revenge.

On the other hand, if you choose to maintain an occupying army instead of colonies, you will spend a fortune. You will waste the entire revenue of the new state just to feed your garrison, turning the conquest into a massive financial loss. Worse, you will infuriate the entire population. Constantly moving an army around disrupts everything and everyone feels the hardship. As a result, the whole population turns hostile. These are enemies who, even though they have been beaten, remain on their own home turf and are still capable of doing real damage. For every possible reason, maintaining a military occupation is useless, whereas planting colonies is highly effective.

Additionally, a prince who occupies a foreign region must make himself the leader and protector of his weaker neighbors. At the same time, he must actively work to weaken the more powerful states in the area. Above all, he must ensure that no foreign power as strong as himself ever gains a foothold there. Whenever a powerful outsider enters a region, it is always because they were invited by discontented locals, driven either by extreme ambition or deep fear. For example, the Romans were invited into Greece by the Aetolians. In fact, everywhere the Romans expanded, they were brought in by the local inhabitants. The pattern is always the same: the moment a powerful foreigner steps into a region, all the weaker states immediately flock to his side, united by their hatred for whoever currently dominates them. The newcomer does not even have to work to win them over; they naturally align with him. His only job is to make sure these weaker allies do not gain too much power or authority. With his own army and their willing support, he can easily crush the stronger states and remain the absolute master of the entire region. Any prince who fails to manage this dynamic will quickly lose whatever he has conquered. And even while he holds it, he will face endless troubles and rebellions.

The Romans followed these rules perfectly in the countries they conquered. They sent out colonies. They allied with the weaker states without letting them grow too strong. They ruthlessly crushed the more powerful states. And they never allowed a strong foreign power to gain influence. Greece is a perfect example of their strategy. The Romans maintained friendly relations with the Achaeans and the Aetolians. They humiliated the Kingdom of Macedonia. They completely drove out King Antiochus. Despite all their loyal service, the Achaeans and Aetolians were never allowed to expand their territories. No amount of persuasion from King Philip could convince the Romans to be his friend until they had thoroughly humbled him first. And no matter how influential Antiochus was, the Romans never let him keep an inch of authority in the region. The Romans did exactly what all smart leaders must do: they looked out not just for current troubles, but for future ones. They used every ounce of their energy to prevent those problems from taking root. If you see a problem coming early, it is easy to fix. If you wait until it is staring you in the face, the medicine will be useless because the disease has become incurable. It is just like doctors say about tuberculosis: in the beginning, the disease is easy to cure but hard to detect. However, if left untreated, it becomes easy to detect but impossible to cure. The same thing happens in politics. If you are wise enough to foresee political threats early, you can crush them quickly. But if you are blind to them and let them grow until everyone can see them, there is no longer any remedy. The Romans foresaw their troubles and dealt with them immediately. They never let a crisis fester just to avoid a war. They knew that you cannot avoid a war; you can only postpone it to your enemy's advantage. They intentionally fought Philip and Antiochus in Greece so they would not have to fight them later on their own soil in Italy. They could have delayed both conflicts, but they refused to do so. They totally rejected the cowardly advice you constantly hear from the so-called wise men of our time, who say to just enjoy the benefits of buying time. Instead, the Romans relied on the benefits of their own courage and sharp judgment. Time changes everything. It can bring good luck, but it can just as easily bring disaster.
Note that we must refer to the earlier remark in the introduction regarding the specific phrasing used for maintaining friendly relations.

Now let us look at France and see if they followed any of these rules. I will focus on King Louis, not Charles, because Louis held onto Italy much longer, making his actions easier to study. You will see that Louis did the exact opposite of everything you are supposed to do to hold onto a mixed principality.
King Louis XII of France was known as The Father of the People. He was born in 1462 and died in 1515.
King Charles VIII of France was born in 1470 and died in 1498.

King Louis was dragged into Italy by the greed of the Venetians, who wanted his military help to carve off half of Lombardy for themselves. I do not necessarily blame the king for this initial move. He wanted to get a foothold in Italy but had zero allies there. Because of the terrible behavior of his predecessor, King Charles, every door was slammed in his face. Louis was forced to take whatever friendships he could get. His plan would have worked perfectly if he had not made a string of massive mistakes later on. Once Louis captured Lombardy, he instantly won back all the prestige that Charles had lost. Genoa surrendered. The Florentines eagerly became his allies. The Marquis of Mantua, the Duke of Ferrara, the Bentivogli, the Lady of Forli, and all the various lords of Faenza, Pesaro, Rimini, Camerino, and Piombino, along with the Lucchese, Pisans, and Sienese, everyone rushed forward begging for his friendship. Only then did the Venetians realize what a reckless, suicidal mistake they had made. Just to grab two measly towns in Lombardy, they had effectively made the King of France the master of two-thirds of Italy.

Think about how easily the king could have maintained his grip on Italy if he had just followed the basic rules I outlined earlier. All he had to do was protect his new, weaker friends. They were numerous, but they were frail and terrified. Some were terrified of the Church, others of the Venetians. Because of this fear, they were absolutely forced to stick by his side. With their combined support, he could have easily crushed any of the remaining strong powers. Instead, the moment he arrived in Milan, he did the exact opposite. He actually helped Pope Alexander invade the Romagna. It completely flew over his head that this suicidal move was weakening his own position. He was actively throwing away allies who had just rushed into his open arms. Worse, he was massively empowering the Church by giving it huge military and political dominance on top of its spiritual authority. Once he made this first fatal error, he was trapped. He eventually had to march back into Italy himself just to stop the Pope's ambition and prevent Alexander from taking over Tuscany.

But apparently, making the Church an unstoppable powerhouse and alienating all his allies was not enough for him. Out of sheer greed for the Kingdom of Naples, Louis decided to split it with the King of Spain. Instead of remaining the ultimate, unchallenged master of Italy, he invited a powerful partner in. This gave all the ambitious opportunists and angry malcontents in the region a new foreign power to rally behind. Louis could have easily left a loyal puppet king in charge of Naples. Instead, he overthrew him, only to replace him with the King of Spain, the very man who would eventually drive Louis out of Italy entirely.

The desire to conquer and expand is perfectly natural and incredibly common. When capable men do it, they are praised, not blamed. But when men lack the power to succeed yet stubbornly try to conquer anyway, that is pure foolishness and deserves nothing but mockery. If France had the military strength to attack Naples on her own, she should have just done it. If she did not have the strength, she never should have divided the kingdom with a rival. You could excuse Louis splitting Lombardy with the Venetians because it gave him his initial foothold in Italy. But splitting Naples with Spain had no such excuse. It was totally unnecessary and completely foolish.

Ultimately, King Louis committed five fatal errors in Italy. He destroyed the weaker powers. He bolstered the strength of an already powerful state. He invited a massive foreign military into the region. He never bothered to move there and live among the people. And he failed to establish any colonies. Amazingly, even with these five catastrophic blunders, he might have survived if he had not committed a sixth: he decided to strip the Venetians of their territories. If he had not already made the Pope invincible and dragged Spain into Italy, crushing the Venetians would have been a smart and necessary move. But because he had already empowered those two giants, he never should have allowed the Venetians to be ruined. As long as Venice remained strong, they would have fiercely blocked anyone else from invading Lombardy. The Venetians would only allow an attack if it made them the masters, and nobody else would steal Lombardy from France just to hand it over to Venice. Nobody had the guts to fight both France and Venice at the same time.

Now, someone might argue that King Louis handed the Romagna to Pope Alexander and split Naples with Spain simply to avoid a war. I will answer that with the same iron rule I stated before: never commit a political blunder just to dodge a war. You can never truly avoid a war; you only delay it, and always to your own severe disadvantage. Someone else might argue that Louis owed the Pope a favor. He promised to help the Pope's military campaign in exchange for the Pope granting him a divorce and giving a Cardinal's hat to the Archbishop of Rouen. To that, I will point to what I write later in this book regarding the promises of princes, and exactly how much they should be respected.
King Louis XII divorced his wife, Jeanne, and married Anne of Brittany in 1499 just to keep the Duchy of Brittany under the control of the French crown.
The Archbishop of Rouen was Georges d'Amboise, who was made a cardinal by Pope Alexander VI. He was born in 1460 and died in 1510.

And that is exactly how King Louis lost Lombardy. He completely ignored every single rule followed by men who successfully conquer and hold territories. There is no mystery or bad luck here; his failure was completely logical and predictable. I actually discussed this directly with the Cardinal of Rouen at Nantes, back when Cesare Borgia, the ruthless son of Pope Alexander, was busy conquering the Romagna. The Cardinal arrogantly told me that Italians simply did not understand war. I fired back that the French clearly did not understand politics. If they did, they never would have allowed the Church to become so dangerously powerful. History has proven my point. France directly created the overwhelming power of both the Church and Spain in Italy, and it was those very powers that ultimately destroyed France's presence there. This leaves us with a golden rule of politics that almost never fails: whoever helps another rise to power is ultimately paving the way for their own ruin. You build them up using either your own cunning or your own military force. Once they reach the top, they will instinctively distrust both your cunning and your force, and they will eliminate you.
